title: Michel Foucault
keyWorks: The Use of Pleasure and The Care of the Self (1984)
summary: Foucault investigated how power works not only through prohibitions but through “norms”: schools, hospitals, questionnaires and grades quietly teach us what to be. He showed that much of what seems “natural” in us has a history — which means it could have been otherwise. In his late work he turned to the ancient “care of the self”: to how a person can give shape to their own life.
onEmotions: Foucault did not build a theory of emotions, but he teaches us to ask our feelings an unexpected question: not only “what’s wrong with me?” but also “where did I get this yardstick?” Many of our shames, anxieties and feelings of inadequacy are traces of “normalization” — society’s habit of comparing everyone to a norm. This view lifts part of the burden: not everything that hurts is your personal fault. And the late Foucault adds that you can treat your feelings as material for “technologies of the self” — calm, attentive work on your own life, without self-punishment.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is an honest response to a world that expects a great deal of you, and there is nothing shameful in it. Foucault described the image of the “panopticon” — a prison designed by Bentham in which the prisoner cannot see the guard and so, just in case, watches himself. This, according to Foucault, is how “disciplinary power” works: it doesn’t need to punish constantly; it is enough that we feel we might be seen and assessed. From this point of view, one might say that part of anxiety is an inner guard: the feeling of an exam that never ends, even when no one is watching. This is not your weakness but a trace of how schools, offices and social media feeds are built. When you notice whose gaze is built into your anxiety, it stops being a verdict on you and becomes information about the world you live in.
anxiety.practice: Write down: whose imagined gaze do you feel right now, and on what scale is it grading you? Who, in your view, invented that scale?

fear.text: Fear is often intelligent: it notices danger before we manage to name it. Foucault wrote little about fear as a feeling, but a great deal about how society draws lines between the “normal” and the “abnormal,” between insiders and the dangerous. In History of Madness he showed that the line between reason and madness shifts over history: in different eras, different people were pushed across it. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that many of our fears — of turning out “not right,” of falling outside the norm, of being excluded — were absorbed together with those lines. But Foucault insisted: power is never total; at every point in it a response is possible. Fear doesn’t mean you are helpless. It can show you where the line runs — and a line you can see is one you can think about, not only fear.
fear.practice: Ask yourself: what am I afraid of — the event itself, or who I’ll be taken for if it happens? Write down both answers.

quote.text: Where there is power, there is resistance.
quote.author: Michel Foucault
quote.source: The Will to Knowledge (The History of Sexuality, vol. 1), 1976

sadness.text: Sadness has a right to a place in your day, even when everyone around you is expected to be “on top of things.” Foucault used the word “normalization” for the way society divides states into healthy and deviant and then gently nudges everyone toward the middle. Today the unspoken norm is to be positive and productive, and next to it sadness looks suspicious. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that the very rush to “fix” sadness is part of this normalization. The late Foucault studied ancient “technologies of the self,” among them the keeping of personal notebooks the Greeks called hypomnemata: books in which a person copied out what they had read and lived through in order to gather themselves. This isn’t treatment or a fight but attentive care. You don’t have to drive sadness out; you can listen to it and write it down — and then it becomes part of your own text rather than a deviation from someone else’s.
sadness.practice: Keep a “hypomnema” for one evening: write three sentences about your sadness and one line from a book or song that resonates with it right now.

grief.text: Grief is one of the deepest human experiences, and no one has the right to set a deadline for it. Foucault noticed something important about our era: modern power, which he called “biopolitics,” is occupied with managing life — health, life expectancy, efficiency. Death, meanwhile, has become the most private, almost hidden moment of existence: it is pushed out of shared space. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that if it seems to you that the people around you expect you to “pull yourself together quickly,” this is not only their callousness but a feature of a culture that leaves little room for loss. You can give grief its place yourself. The ancient “technologies of the self” Foucault studied are precisely practices a person creates for themselves, without waiting for permission: rituals, letters, reflections, conversations with those close to you.
grief.practice: What small ritual of remembrance could you create — not “the proper way,” but the way that you in particular need?

loneliness.text: Loneliness truly hurts, and behind it lies an understandable need for others. Foucault showed that disciplinary power “individualizes”: it distributes people into separate places, files, rows in a table — each one apart, each one comparable. From this point of view, one might say that part of loneliness is not your personal failure but an effect of a world that has sorted us into cells. Interestingly, in studying the ancient “care of the self,” Foucault stressed that it was never a solitary affair. Seneca wrote letters to Lucilius, students talked with their teachers, friends helped each other see themselves. The care of the self, for Foucault, doesn’t isolate; it strengthens the bonds between people. So reaching out to others when you are lonely is not weakness but the very essence of that care.
loneliness.practice: Write a short letter — as Seneca did to Lucilius — to someone you would like to talk about life with. You don’t have to send it.

anger.text: Anger is a legitimate signal: something has touched your boundaries or your sense of justice. Foucault wrote that discipline produces “docile bodies” — useful, convenient, predictable people. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that anger is often the first bodily sign that something in you refuses to be merely convenient. In his lecture “What Is Critique?” he defined the critical attitude as the art of not being governed in just any way, at any price. This is not a call to destruction, nor a reason to shame yourself for anger. Rather, it is an invitation to turn anger into a precise question: exactly what way of being treated am I protesting against? Once the answer is found, anger stops being a vague heat and becomes knowledge of what matters to you.
anger.practice: Finish the sentence: “I don’t want to be treated like this: …” — and look at what lies behind that “like this.”

quote.text: …the art of not being governed quite so much.
quote.author: Michel Foucault

shame.text: Shame is one of the most painful feelings, and if it is with you now, that is hard. Foucault described the “examination” — a technique that combines observation and assessment: everyone is compared with everyone, ranked, and their deviations noted. He called this “normalizing judgment.” From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that shame is often the feeling of having failed the exam on the norm. He also showed that our culture has taught people to look for “the truth about themselves” in what is most secret and shameful, as in confession. But the norm is a historical invention, not a law of nature: it has a date of birth and authors. This doesn’t cancel your actions or your responsibility, but it lets you separate what you actually did from someone else’s yardstick that you carry inside.
shame.practice: Name the norm before which you feel ashamed, and ask: how old is it, who set it, and whom does it benefit?

quote.text: The soul is the prison of the body.
quote.author: Michel Foucault

guilt.text: Guilt shows that you care how your actions affect others — it is a valuable feeling. Foucault compared two ways of looking at one’s mistakes. Christian confession, as he described it, taught people to decipher their own sinfulness endlessly. But the ancient Stoic Seneca, whose evening reviews of the day Foucault analyzed in detail, looked at his lapses not as a judge passing sentence but more like an administrator checking what was done well and what could be adjusted next time. The aim of such a “technology of the self” is not to punish yourself but to fine-tune your conduct. From this point of view, guilt can become not an endless trial of yourself but a calm stocktaking: what happened, what I can fix, what it teaches me.
guilt.practice: Go over one situation “as an administrator”: what I wanted, what happened, what I’ll do differently — without using the word “bad.”

envy.text: Envy is a very human feeling, and there is nothing monstrous in it. Foucault showed that disciplinary society is a society of ranks: tables, grades and ratings make everyone visible and comparable. In his lectures The Birth of Biopolitics he described the person of the neoliberal age as an “entrepreneur of himself,” constantly investing in his “human capital.” From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that in such a world envy is almost built into the structure of life: we are continually comparing our “capitals.” This doesn’t make envy good or bad — it explains why it is so sharp. The late Foucault offered a different measure: life as a work with its own style, not as a place in someone else’s table. Envy can then hint at what you want, but it doesn’t have to decide the scale by which you live.
envy.practice: What exactly do you envy — a thing, a way of life, or a place in a ranking? What ranking would you never draw up yourself?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can be very heavy, and feeling them doesn’t make you any less. The late Foucault spoke of an “aesthetics of existence”: for the ancient Greeks, ethics was not a code of rules but work on oneself, like an artist’s work on a piece. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that emptiness sometimes sets in when ready-made forms of life — fulfilled expectations, “correct” roles — stop filling you. This is not necessarily a breakdown; it may be an unfilled part of the canvas. Foucault didn’t propose grand plans: technologies of the self are small, repeated practices through which a life gradually takes shape. You don’t need to cram emptiness with whatever comes to hand. You can simply ask which small actions give you even a faint sense of your own style.
emptiness.practice: Choose one small action for tomorrow that you will do not “because you have to” but as a brushstroke in your life as a work of art.

quote.text: But couldn’t everyone’s life become a work of art?
quote.author: Michel Foucault

confusion.text: Confusion is natural when familiar landmarks stop working. Foucault himself disliked fixed identities and definitions. His method, “genealogy,” shows that what seems eternal and natural — from the notion of “normality” to our ideas about ourselves — has a history and could have turned out differently. From Foucault’s point of view, confusion is not only a misfortune but also a moment when the seams show: you notice that many of the categories you used to describe yourself were stitched together by someone, at some point. Foucault called critique work “at the limits” — where we test what in us is necessary and what is contingent. Confusion can be such a limit. You don’t have to quickly find a new final formula for yourself; you can stay in this opening a while and see what becomes visible in it.
confusion.practice: Write down one thing about yourself that you considered “natural” and now doubt. When, and from whom, did you absorb it?

quote.text: Do not ask who I am and do not ask me to remain the same.
quote.author: Michel Foucault

fatigue.text: Fatigue and burnout are not laziness or a flaw of character but a living creature’s response to overload. Foucault described in detail how discipline organizes time: schedules broken into segments, the principle of “not wasting a minute,” the drive to use the body’s time as fully as possible. Later he showed how this logic expands: the neoliberal “entrepreneur of himself” optimizes his whole life. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say burnout is the place where the body refuses to be endlessly useful. Importantly, the ancient “care of the self” that Foucault studied was not self-optimization. It included solitude, walks, conversations, reading, pauses — time that owes nothing to anyone. Rest, seen this way, is not a reward for productivity but the very practice of relating to yourself.
fatigue.practice: Find five minutes in today that won’t be “used” for anything. Notice how hard it is not to fill them.

boredom.text: Boredom is not a whim but a signal worth listening to. Foucault described “disciplinary time”: a day broken into identical segments, exercises repeated according to a set scheme, a life where every movement is scheduled in advance. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say boredom often appears when we live inside a form we didn’t choose and repeat someone else’s routine. The late Foucault spoke not of great revolutions but of “practices of freedom” — small shifts in the everyday through which a person begins to decide for themselves how to live. Boredom offers a pause in which the form becomes visible. You don’t need to rush off in search of strong sensations; it is enough to notice where the schedule has become your prison and shift it a little.
boredom.practice: Do one habitual thing slightly differently — by another route, in a different order — and notice what has changed in how it feels.

joy.text: Joy needs no justification — neither usefulness nor merit. Foucault was often considered a gloomy thinker, but he thought a great deal about pleasures. In The Will to Knowledge he proposed relying not on imposed schemes of “correct” desire but on “bodies and pleasures” — on what is experienced directly. In The Use of Pleasure he showed that the ancient Greeks saw pleasures not as sin or commodity but as material for the art of living: the question was not “is it permitted?” but “how can this be enjoyed beautifully and with measure?” From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that joy no one grades and that serves no purpose is a small territory of freedom from normalization. It doesn’t need to be put on display or turned into productivity. It can simply be lived.
joy.practice: Notice one pleasure in today that serves nothing and is graded by no one. Let it remain yours alone.

love.text: Tenderness and love are among the most precious experiences, even when they don’t fit into familiar frames. Foucault showed that even what is most intimate in us is organized: around love and sexuality there are “apparatuses” (dispositifs) — networks of advice, institutions and ideas that suggest how to love “properly.” In the interview “Friendship as a Way of Life” he spoke of people having to invent relationships for which there are not yet ready-made forms or names, and he saw this not as a problem but as a creative task. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say: if your tenderness doesn’t match the template — too quiet, too strange, not “leading” anywhere — that is not a mistake. It is a space in which you yourself give form to your connections.
love.practice: Describe your love or tenderness in two or three sentences without using a single ready-made relationship label.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm and important feeling, and it’s good that it is with you. Foucault didn’t write about gratitude directly, but in his last lectures he thought a great deal about “parrhesia” — the ancient Greek notion of courageous, frank speech, when a person tells another the truth at the risk of the relationship or their own standing. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that among the most precious gifts are those brought to us by people who dared to be honest. There is another thought in his spirit: gratitude shouldn’t be turned into yet another norm — “be grateful,” “keep a gratitude journal or there’s something wrong with you.” Then it becomes a discipline. Living gratitude is free: it comes by itself and asks for no report.
gratitude.practice: Remember someone who once told you a hard truth. What are you grateful to them for now, with time having passed?

hope.text: Hope is a needed feeling, even when it is fragile. Foucault was skeptical of grand promises of final liberation, but his philosophy is, in its own way, very hopeful. Genealogy shows that what seems unchangeable arose in history, and so it can change. Foucault said that his position leads not to apathy but to active, sober engagement: since nothing is guaranteed, there is always something to do. From this point of view, hope is not waiting for someone to come and fix everything but knowing that the world is not closed and there is still room in it for your step. It doesn’t require optimism about everything at once; one small place where you can do something is enough.
hope.practice: Name one thing that seems unchangeable right now. When and how did it come about? What small part of it can you shift?

quote.text: My point is not that everything is bad, but that everything is dangerous… If everything is dangerous, then we always have something to do.
quote.author: Michel Foucault

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a tender and understandable feeling: we long for what once held us. Foucault was a historian, but not a nostalgic one at all. In his essay “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” he criticized the search for a “pure origin” — a golden beginning from which everything went wrong: the past, in his view, was never whole and flawless. But he valued the past for something else: its difference shows that the present is not the only possibility. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that nostalgia can be read not as longing for a lost paradise but as knowledge that life can be arranged differently. Then the past becomes not a place you can’t return to but a hint at what you can invent here and now.
nostalgia.practice: What exactly do you love about the past? What small piece of it could you not bring back but reinvent in your life today?

craving.text: A sharp “I want it right now” can sweep over you completely, and there is nothing shameful in that. In The Use of Pleasure (1984), the late Foucault studied how the ancient Greeks related to desires. He was struck that their ethics was built not on prohibitions but on enkrateia — self-mastery, the ability not to become a slave to one’s pleasures. What mattered to the Greeks was not shame but a question of measure and timing: not “is it good to desire?” but “who is the master here — me or the desire?” Freedom for them meant not the absence of desires but that desire doesn’t decide for you. From this point of view, a wave of craving needs neither to be cursed nor obeyed at once. You can watch it the way you watch the weather: it rises, peaks and subsides.
craving.practice: When the wave comes, set a timer for five minutes and simply note how its strength changes: stronger, the same, weaker.

addiction.text: When life has long revolved around one thing, it is exhausting — and it is not a moral failure. Foucault wrote a great deal about how society turns a person into a “case” and hangs on them a category that starts to eclipse everything else. He reminded us that a human being is never reducible to a label. Studying ancient “technologies of the self,” the late Foucault described hypomnemata — notebooks in which Greeks and Romans recorded thoughts and observations in order to give shape to their lives gradually, day by day. This was not confession or self-punishment but patient work. From this point of view, leaving a long-standing cycle is not one heroic leap but many small practices of freedom. They are often easier to do together with others — for example, in a mutual-help group.
addiction.practice: Start a small notebook and write one observation about today in it — without judgment, as a note to yourself.

hangover.text: The morning after is heavy in both body and soul: anxiety, shame, gaps in memory. Right now you are allowed to be gentle with yourself. In his lectures on “technologies of the self” (1982), Foucault compared two ways of dealing with the day that has passed. Christian confession, he wrote, required searching out hidden sins in oneself and confessing them. Seneca, by contrast, went over his day every evening quite differently: not as a judge passing sentence but as a manager checking the accounts and calmly noting what to do differently next time. From this point of view, a “moral hangover” often resembles an inner interrogation. But you can choose the manager’s stance: not to extract guilt from yourself but to note what happened and what will be useful tomorrow. This doesn’t cancel responsibility, but it removes the self-trial.
hangover.practice: When you feel a little better, write two lines: “What happened” and “What I’ll make a note of” — in the tone of a manager, not a judge.

euphoria.text: A burst when everything seems possible is a vivid experience, and you can simply enjoy it. Foucault has a thought that resonates with this feeling. The main lesson of his work is that what seems natural and unchangeable to us has a history — and so could have been otherwise. In his essay “What Is Enlightenment?” (1984) he described philosophy as a testing of the limits imposed on us and a search for the possibility of going beyond them. From this point of view, euphoria is a bodily experience that limits are movable and the world is open. At the same time the late Foucault, following the Greeks, valued measure and long-term “work on oneself” more than brief bursts. So euphoria can not only be lived through but also kept: you can remember what possibility it showed you.
euphoria.practice: Write in one sentence which limit seems movable to you right now. Not as a plan, but as an image.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a vivid evening — can be very hard, and it is not your fault. In Discipline and Punish (1975), Foucault showed how modern society trains us in an even, controlled rhythm — schedules, productivity norms. Against this background any drop is easily read as a deviation from the norm, a breakdown. But from Foucault’s point of view you can ask: whose norm is it that demands you always be steady and upbeat? Studying the ancient Stoics, the late Foucault described “askesis” not as a heroic feat but as calm daily exercises that help one get through both highs and lows. From this point of view, the comedown is not a verdict but a time for small, unhurried actions.
crash.practice: Choose one simple act of care for your body — eat something, step outside, wash your face — and do it slowly.

panic.text: A wave of panic is a genuinely frightening experience: your heart, your breathing, the feeling that something irreparable is about to happen. Foucault didn’t write about panic attacks, but from his point of view one could say this. In Discipline and Punish (1975) he showed how disciplinary society trains the body to be “docile” — manageable, composed, always under control. That’s why the moment the body slips out of control is doubly frightening. The late Foucault turned to the ancient “care of the self,” which included care of the body — attention to breathing, routine, simple exercises. Not suppression, but gentle attention. From this point of view, in a panic you can stop fighting your body and instead take care of it. A wave like this usually rises and subsides within a few minutes.
panic.practice: Put your feet flat on the floor and feel the support. Name five objects around you out loud, and make your exhale longer than your inhale.

dread.text: Dread before the abyss, the question “what’s the point of it all?” — this is a deep experience, and there’s no need to be ashamed of it. In The Order of Things (1966), Foucault described how modern thought is built on an “analytic of finitude”: it is precisely because human beings are finite and limited that they are able to know and to ask at all. Finitude is not a defect but a condition of thinking. The late Foucault added that the meaning of life is not given to us in advance but can be created — he proposed treating one’s own life as a “work of art,” made gradually, day by day. From this point of view, the question “what for?” is not proof of meaninglessness but the beginning of work. The answer doesn’t have to come at once; it is built from small deeds, relationships, attachments.
dread.practice: Write down one small thing you did or saw today that was even a little dear to you.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives and you’re not where you should be is very common, and it isn’t only about you. In Discipline and Punish (1975), Foucault described the “panopticon” — a prison where the inmate can always be seen by the guard and therefore starts watching himself. Today we are like inhabitants of a panopticon in reverse: we constantly see other people’s lives and compare our own with them. Foucault called this kind of mechanism “normalization”: the endless comparison of everyone against an average yardstick. From this point of view, the fear of missing out is not your inadequacy but a consequence of this machine of visibility. And here lies relief: what you are shown is not the whole truth about other people’s lives but a shop window.
fomo.practice: Notice whose life you compare yours with most often, and ask: “What am I seeing — a life or a shop window?”

sleepless.text: Sleepless hours when your thoughts won’t let go can be very lonely. In Discipline and Punish (1975), Foucault showed how modern society built disciplinary time: schedules, deadlines, the use of every minute. Later he wrote about “biopower” — power that concerns itself with the life, health and productivity of the population. Sleep, too, has become part of this logic: it has to be properly “replenished” so that you work well tomorrow. From this point of view, one might say that nighttime anxiety is often the voice of the same norm: “you won’t get enough sleep, you won’t cope.” That doesn’t make insomnia your fault or your failure. The night doesn’t have to become an exam: even quiet rest without sleep is still rest.
sleepless.practice: Tell yourself: “Right now I don’t need to get anything done.” Write your anxious thoughts on a sheet of paper, one line each, and set them aside until morning.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply because it strikes at trust — the thing closeness rests on. In his last lectures (1983–1984), Foucault explored “parrhesia” — the ancient art of frank speech. For the Greeks, telling a friend the truth meant taking a risk: opening up, saying something that might harm you yourself. Such frankness is possible only where there is trust. From this point of view, betrayal is the breaking of that unspoken pact in which you opened up and took a risk. Foucault also wrote about “friendship as a way of life” — about bonds people create themselves, without ready-made rules. This means relationships are always a creative act, not a guarantee. Your pain is a trace of what you truly invested in this relationship.
betrayal.practice: Write down what you were frank about with this person. Your capacity for frankness is yours; it hasn’t been taken from you.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonizing: the fear of losing someone close makes everything inside you clench. Foucault distinguished “relations of power” from “states of domination.” Power, for Foucault, is present in all relationships, even in love, and that isn’t necessarily bad: in living relationships it is mobile and reversible, a game in which both are free. Domination is when the game freezes and one person tries to control the other completely. From this point of view, jealousy can be understood as the wish to stop the moving game and fix it forever — because uncertainty is frightening. This is a very human wish, and there’s no need to be ashamed of it. But Foucault would remind you: the aliveness of a relationship consists precisely in both people remaining free. Fear is part of that price.
jealousy.practice: Write down what exactly you want to “lock in” in this relationship, and what the other person’s freedom means to you.

resentment.text: Long-held resentment is heavy, and if you carry it, you really were hurt. In his essay “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” (1971), Foucault described “genealogy” — a way of looking at what seems eternal and unchanging as something that took shape from accidents, coincidences, particular events. You can apply this view to resentment too. It seems part of you, as if it had always been there and always will be. But it has a history: when it appeared, what fed it, how it changed. This view doesn’t require you to forgive or forget. It simply lets you see resentment as a history rather than a fate — and then it can have a continuation that you write yourself.
resentment.practice: Write a short “genealogy” of your resentment: when it appeared, what fed it, how it has changed over time.

heartbreak.text: A breakup can feel like the collapse of a whole world, and that pain deserves to be acknowledged. In the interview “Friendship as a Way of Life” (1981), Foucault observed that our society offers very few recognized forms of intimacy — essentially, the couple and the family. When a couple falls apart, it seems everything collapses, since there appear to be no other forms for love and connection. Foucault called for inventing new relationships — friendships, alliances, attachments that don’t yet have names. From this point of view, the end of a relationship is an enormous loss, but not the end of your capacity for closeness. Love and connection can take many forms, and some of them are already in your life — it’s just not customary to count them as the main ones.
heartbreak.practice: Write down the names of people with whom you have any kind of closeness — even if it isn’t the kind of relationship usually called the main one.

impostor.text: The fear of being found out any minute is familiar to a great many people, including those who are doing perfectly well. In Discipline and Punish (1975), Foucault showed how the “examination” works: a technique combining observation and assessment that turns a person into a “case” with scores and marks. We’ve grown used to the idea that our worth must be constantly confirmed by someone above us. From this point of view, impostor syndrome is life inside an endless exam, where any moment might turn out to be a test. And in the essay “The Subject and Power” (1982), Foucault proposed not searching for one’s “true essence” but refusing imposed forms of identity. Perhaps you don’t need to prove you are “the real thing.” It is enough to do what you do.
impostor.practice: Ask yourself: “Who is this imaginary examiner?” Describe them in one sentence — and notice that you are not obliged to sit their exam.

quote.text: Maybe the target nowadays is not to discover what we are, but to refuse what we are.
quote.author: Michel Foucault

self_hatred.text: When your inner voice is merciless, living with it is very hard, and you deserve gentleness. Foucault showed that the panopticon works most effectively once the guard is no longer needed: the person becomes their own overseer. The inner critic resembles such a guard who has moved in. Studying history, the late Foucault noticed something else too: the Christian tradition taught people to search for sin in themselves and renounce themselves, while the ancient “care of the self” was entirely different — a careful kind of work in which a person treats themselves as someone to be cared for, not someone to be punished. From this point of view, self-hatred is not the truth about you but one historically formed way of relating to yourself. There are others.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence your inner critic says, and ask: “Is this the voice of a guard, or of someone who cares for me?”

helplessness.text: Feeling powerless to change anything can be very hard, and it deserves to be taken seriously. Foucault proposed a different way of looking at power: it is not concentrated entirely somewhere at the top but dispersed across a multitude of small relationships — in families, at work, in conversations. This means not everything has been decided for us. Foucault spoke of “practices of freedom”: even where big changes are out of reach, small possibilities remain for acting differently — in how you speak, whom you spend time with, how you treat yourself. From this point of view, helplessness is a real experience, but not the whole truth. You are not all-powerful, but you are not entirely powerless either: between these extremes lies the space where freedom lives.
helplessness.practice: Write down one small action that is within your power today — even if it seems insignificant.

procrastination.text: When you just can’t get started, it’s easy to call yourself lazy. In Discipline and Punish (1975), Foucault showed how disciplinary society built an “exhaustive use of time”: schedules in which every minute must be useful and a person always productive. We have absorbed these demands so deeply that any delay feels like failure. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that procrastination is sometimes the body’s quiet resistance to this regime rather than a flaw of character. That doesn’t mean the task needn’t be done. But you can ease the pressure: instead of forcing yourself heroically, try a small exercise, as the Stoics did — one action, without self-punishment.
procrastination.practice: Set a timer for five minutes and do the smallest part of the task. When it rings, you are free to stop.

uprooted.text: When the ground has gone from under your feet — a move, emigration, the loss of a familiar world — it is a deep loss, even if the decision was right. In his lecture “Of Other Spaces” (1967), Foucault described “heterotopias” — special places where the ordinary order of things is simultaneously reflected and inverted. He considered the ship the finest example: a place without a place, floating between shores. Life after a move is like such a space: you are no longer there and not yet here. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say this position also carries a special kind of knowledge: you see that the norms of both the old world and the new one are not laws of nature but historical habits. This doesn’t cancel the longing, but it gives you the freedom to choose what to take with you from both worlds.
uprooted.practice: Write down one habit from your former place and one from the new place that you would like to keep both of.

overload.text: The endless stream of information and feeds really is exhausting. In The Will to Knowledge (1976), Foucault made an unexpected discovery: modern power works not so much through prohibition and silence as through an “incitement to discourse” — to endless talking, confessing, explaining. We aren’t forced to be silent; we are made to speak all the time, to display, and to consume what others have said. From this point of view, overload is not your inability to keep up but a consequence of an arrangement in which the stream must never stop. The late Foucault, following the Stoics, valued selection: reading little, but attentively, and copying out what you really need. You can allow yourself not to know everything.
overload.practice: From today’s stream, copy out one thought that will really be useful to you, and close the rest.

unreality.text: The sense that everything around you, or you yourself, is somehow not quite real can be frightening, and it deserves gentle care. In History of Madness (1961), Foucault showed that the line between “normal” and “strange” experience is not eternal: different eras drew it differently, and those who went through unusual experiences were often simply silenced. He also analyzed Descartes’ Meditations, in which the philosopher seriously asks whether he might be dreaming everything. From this point of view, your experience is part of a long human history of doubting reality, one that philosophers have thought about too. It doesn’t make you alien or “wrong.” It can be talked about rather than hidden — and speaking of it often helps you find your way back.
unreality.practice: Describe three things around you, out loud or on paper, as concretely as possible: color, shape, temperature.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience, and you can simply let it fill you. In the interview “The Masked Philosopher” (1980), Foucault said he valued curiosity in the old sense: a readiness to find one’s surroundings strange and remarkable, to break away from the familiar and look at the same things differently. He was also interested in “limit-experiences” — experiences in which a person momentarily steps beyond the bounds of the self. From this point of view, awe is one form of such experience: familiar yardsticks disappear, and the world seems unexpected again. In these minutes your usual norms and judgments briefly recede. Nothing needs to be added to this moment; it is enough to let it last.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with what filled you with awe, without taking a photo or searching for words.

relief.text: Relief, when something heavy lets go, deserves to be noticed. Foucault wrote a great deal about how we live under constant observation and assessment: exams, reports, other people’s expectations. Often relief is precisely the moment when the exam is over and the guard’s gaze has turned away for a while. In that moment you can notice how much strength went into holding on. From Foucault’s point of view, relief is not only a pleasant feeling but also a clue: it shows what exactly was pressing on you. And the late Foucault, drawing on the ancient “care of the self,” would remind you: rest and recovery are not a reward for work but part of how a person builds their life.
relief.practice: Take a long exhale and write one line: “It’s let go now…” — and finish it with what exactly.

calm.text: Calm is a precious state; you can simply stay in it. In his lectures The Hermeneutics of the Subject (1981–1982), Foucault examined in detail how ancient philosophers — Seneca, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius — practiced “retreat into oneself.” This is not an escape from the world but the ability to return to yourself in the midst of your affairs, to find an inner place where you can rest. Seneca urged “claiming yourself for yourself,” and Foucault saw in this one of the central ideas of the “care of the self”: a person belongs not only to their duties but also to themselves. From this point of view, your calm is not idleness but a small practice of freedom. It doesn’t need to be justified by usefulness or results.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute, noticing your breath, and tell yourself: “Right now I belong to myself.”

inspiration.text: Inspiration — the moment when thought flows on its own and you want to create — is one of the best sides of life. In the introduction to The Use of Pleasure (1984), Foucault admitted that what he valued most in thinking was the chance to “get free of oneself,” to think differently than one thought before. He spoke of life as a “work of art” and of an “aesthetics of existence” — the art of giving form to one’s own life. From this point of view, inspiration is not a rare gift of the chosen few but a moment when this capacity suddenly becomes palpable: you see that it is possible to think and live differently. You don’t have to shape it into a result right away. It is enough to give it room and write it down while it is fresh.
inspiration.practice: Write down what came to you as it is, without editing — as a note in your notebook.

quote.text: There are times in life when the question of knowing if one can think differently than one thinks, and perceive differently than one sees, is absolutely necessary if one is to go on looking and reflecting at all.
quote.author: Michel Foucault

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is an uncomfortable feeling, but almost everyone knows it, and by itself it doesn’t make you a bad person. Foucault showed that modern society is built as a system of constant comparison: grades, ratings and tables place everyone relative to others. He called this “normalizing judgment.” From Foucault’s point of view, one might say: in a world where everyone is ranked all the time, someone else’s failure is involuntarily felt as a small step up in your own table. Schadenfreude is partly an echo of this system, not only a personal trait of yours. Understanding this doesn’t excuse cruelty, but it removes needless shame. And it prompts a question: what competition am I taking part in without ever having chosen to?
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: in which ranking did someone else’s failure make me feel “better”? Who invented that ranking, and when?

contempt.text: Contempt gives a sense of superiority and safety: I am not like that. All his life Foucault studied how society draws lines between the “normal” and the “abnormal” — the mad, criminals, those who deviate from the norm. In History of Madness he showed how modern reason defined itself by separating and locking away what it considered unreasonable. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say contempt often works in a similar way: we affirm ourselves through those we place beneath us. This doesn’t make you bad, but it shows that contempt may be less knowledge about the other than a way of holding on to your own “norm.” A useful question: what boundary in me is this contempt guarding, and what am I afraid of if it were gone?
contempt.practice: Name a quality you despise in someone else. Then ask: what would I be afraid of if I discovered it in myself?

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong, almost bodily feeling, and it often has its reasons. Foucault showed that much of what seems naturally “normal” or “abnormal” to us has a history: norms take shape and change. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that disgust, too, is partly learned: society teaches us what to consider unclean, dangerous, indecent. It helps to distinguish disgust that protects you from real harm from disgust that repeats other people’s norms. This is especially true of disgust toward yourself: it often speaks in the voice of a culture that has taught us to be ashamed of the body, of weakness, of deviations. You can learn to hear that voice — and disagree with it.
disgust.practice: Ask your disgust: “How do I know this is disgusting?” Write down whose voice you heard in the answer.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is a natural reaction to injustice, and there is nothing shameful in it. Foucault opened Discipline and Punish with a description of an eighteenth-century public execution — a spectacle in which the vengeance of power fell upon a body. He showed how society gradually gave up such spectacles, but not punishment: it became quieter and went deeper. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that revenge is also a desire for power, a desire to regain the strength that was taken from you. That is understandable. But in his preface to Deleuze and Guattari’s Anti-Oedipus, Foucault warned: don’t fall in love with power. Perhaps real strength lies not in punishing but in freeing yourself from the role the person who hurt you imposed on you.
revenge.practice: Ask yourself: what exactly was taken from me — strength, dignity, voice? How can I reclaim it without harming anyone?

quote.text: Do not become enamored of power.
quote.author: Michel Foucault
quote.source: Preface to the English edition of Deleuze and Guattari’s Anti-Oedipus (1977)

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those closest to you is an ordinary, if painful, part of intimacy; afterward it often brings shame. Foucault showed that power belongs not only to the state: it runs through all relationships, even the warmest — between spouses, between parents and children. He called this the “microphysics of power.” At the same time he stressed that power relations are not evil in themselves: in any closeness people influence one another, argue, give way. The trouble is when this mobile game freezes into domination. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that anger at a loved one often signals that something in the relationship has frozen — someone always decides, someone always gives way. This is not a reason to cause pain but a reason to notice the game and speak about it calmly.
anger_at_loved.practice: Once the anger subsides, ask: what has frozen in our relationship? Put it into one calm sentence you could say out loud.

ambivalence.text: Mixed feelings toward someone close — love and irritation, tenderness and fatigue all at once — are a very common state. We’ve been taught to think there must be one “truth” about our feelings inside us. Foucault showed where this habit came from: Christian confession, and later medicine and psychology, taught people to search themselves for a hidden truth and confess it. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that the question “what do I really feel?” becomes a trap if it demands a single final answer. Your relationships are not a riddle to be deciphered but a living practice that you create. Both sides of your feelings can be true, and you can work with both.
ambivalence.practice: Instead of asking “what do I really feel?”, ask: “How do I want to build this relationship today?”

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a loss — a breakup, the end of a loved one’s long illness — often comes together with guilt. This is understandable, and it doesn’t cancel your love. Foucault showed how society uses norms to tell us what it is “normal” to feel and do. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that grief, too, has unspoken norms: how it should look, how long it should last, what is permissible in it. Shame about relief is often shame before a norm rather than before real people. The norm demands a single pure feeling, but life is more complicated. If you spent a long time caring, worrying, carrying a heavy load, relief is a natural response. It doesn’t contradict love; it speaks of how much you have endured.
guilty_relief.practice: Name the “rule” that says relief is out of place right now. Where does it come from? Does it fit your actual story?

indifference.text: Sometimes you aren’t moved by what “should” move you, and that is frightening. Foucault showed how thoroughly our lives are permeated by norms, and from his point of view one might say that feelings have norms too: society expects certain reactions — joy at a celebration, tears in grief, agitation at the news. We are constantly checking ourselves for compliance. Fear of your own indifference is often the fear of failing the exam for being a “normal” person. But feelings don’t have to follow a schedule. Indifference can be exhaustion, protection, a temporary pause. The late Foucault wrote about the “care of the self” — an attentive, not punishing, way of relating to oneself. You can simply notice your state without turning it into a verdict.
indifference.practice: Replace the question “why don’t I feel what I should?” with “what do I need right now?” — and answer it.

escape.text: The urge to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — often arises when life feels like a cage. Foucault described society as a network of institutions — schools, factories, barracks, offices — that order people’s time, bodies and behavior. He called this “discipline.” From Foucault’s point of view, one might say the urge to escape can be a response to this pressure, a signal that you are tired of living by someone else’s timetable. Foucault also wrote about “heterotopias” — “other places” such as a garden, a library, a fair, a ship, where the usual order seems suspended. Sometimes you need a real escape; sometimes it is enough to find your own heterotopia. Either way, it helps to ask: exactly what routine do I want to leave?
escape.practice: Find one “other place” in your week — where the routine is different, even for an hour. How could you be there more often?

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is unavailable or “not the right one” is disorienting. Foucault studied how people in different eras related to desire. He showed that the ancient Greeks thought of it not as a sin to be confessed but as a force one must learn to handle wisely: the question was not “what is forbidden?” but “how do I want to live with this force?” Later the Christian tradition made desire an object of confession and suspicion. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that attraction in itself is neither a crime nor a diagnosis. It is part of your life, which you can approach as material for reflecting on what kind of life you want to build.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down what this attraction says about your life right now: what is missing from it, or what is asking to come out?

quote.text: Freedom is the ontological condition of ethics. But ethics is the considered form that freedom takes when it is informed by reflection.
quote.author: Michel Foucault
quote.source: Interview “The Ethics of the Concern for Self as a Practice of Freedom” (1984)

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment can be paralyzing. Foucault described the “panopticon” — a prison design in which a guard in a central tower can see everyone, while the prisoners never know whether they are being watched at that moment. As a result, they begin to watch themselves. Foucault believed modern society is largely built this way: we constantly feel an evaluating gaze upon us — and become our own guards. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say social anxiety is not a personal defect but partly an echo of this system. Understanding this doesn’t cancel the fear, but it lets you see that the guard inside is not you but a voice that can be noticed and named.
social_anxiety.practice: When it feels as if everyone is watching, ask yourself: who is actually looking at me right now? Notice the real glances, not the imagined ones.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is draining: you can’t tell what will happen. Foucault took a keen interest in ancient exercises designed for exactly such situations. The Stoics practiced praemeditatio malorum, the “premeditation of evils”: calmly imagining possible difficulties so as to meet them prepared rather than caught off guard. Foucault described this as one of the “technologies of the self” — practices through which a person shapes their own relationship to life. He also always stressed that what exists now is not eternal; everything has a history and can change. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that uncertainty is also openness. The future isn’t written in advance, and there is room in it for your freedom.
uncertainty.practice: Calmly write down what might go wrong, and next to it what you would do in that case. Then set the page aside.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, results, news — can be agonizing. Foucault showed how disciplinary society manages time: schedules, deadlines, queues, stages of review. We have been trained to live by someone else’s clock and wait to be assessed. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that part of what makes waiting so painful is that time seems to belong to someone else — whoever decides and replies. The late Foucault studied how ancient philosophers reclaimed their time: they kept notebooks, copied out thoughts, practiced reflection. These notes were not a report to anyone but a way of gathering oneself. Waiting can, at least in part, be turned into your own time — not empty, but filled with what you have chosen yourself.
waiting.practice: While you wait, start a little notebook: each day, write in it one thought you liked.

regret.text: Regret about what you did or didn’t do can gnaw at you for a long time. Foucault distinguished two ways of looking at one’s past. One is tied to Christian confession: searching for sin in oneself, confessing it and bearing the guilt. The other is ancient: every evening Seneca calmly reviewed the day he had lived, but, as Foucault stressed, not as a judge passing sentence — rather as a manager checking the accounts, so as to notice what didn’t work and do better tomorrow. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that regret is useful when it helps you act differently and agonizing when it turns into an endless trial of yourself. You have every right to choose the second, ancient path — the path of care of the self.
regret.practice: In the evening, review the day like a calm manager: what didn’t work, and what will you do differently tomorrow? No verdict on yourself.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person can be sharp: you miss their voice, their habits, their presence. The late Foucault studied the ancient practice of hypomnemata — personal notebooks in which people copied out thoughts, readings and memories in order to keep them close. In his essay “Self Writing” he also described correspondence — for example, Seneca’s letters to his friend Lucilius — as a way of caring for oneself and for one’s connection with another person. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say longing is a form of connection that continues in absence. You can not only endure it but also carefully keep it: write, remember, put it into words. Writing turns the pain of absence into an ongoing conversation.
longing.practice: Write a short letter to this person — you don’t have to send it. Tell them what happened today.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from grim news, wars, injustice — can be very heavy. It is a sign that you care. All his life Foucault concerned himself with those society preferred not to notice: prisoners, people in psychiatric hospitals, the excluded. He didn’t only write: together with others he founded the Prisons Information Group, which collected and published the testimony of prisoners themselves. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that pain for the world is the beginning of attention. And Foucault reminded us that you don’t have to be sad in order to fight injustice. You can carry this pain without letting it extinguish your joy and strength. A small act of attention to a concrete injustice near you is already a response.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small, concrete way to help someone near you. And allow yourself one joy today — that is not a betrayal.

quote.text: Do not think that one has to be sad in order to be militant, even though the thing one is fighting is abominable.
quote.author: Michel Foucault
quote.source: Preface to the English edition of Deleuze and Guattari’s Anti-Oedipus (1977)

rejection.text: Rejection wounds deeply: it feels as though you’ve been tested and found wanting. Foucault described the “examination” — a technique combining observation and assessment that turns a person into a “case” assigned scores and a place in the ranks. School, work, even dating are in many ways built like endless exams. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say rejection feels so heavy because we are used to seeing every “no” as an assessment of the whole person. But the decision of another person or an organization is not an objective verdict; it is a choice made by their own criteria and in their own circumstances. Those criteria have a history and limits. You are more than the result of one exam.
rejection.practice: Write down the criteria by which you weren’t chosen. Then write which of your qualities those criteria didn’t measure at all.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can be very strong and long-standing — sometimes it stretches back to childhood. In the interview “Friendship as a Way of Life,” Foucault said that our society recognizes only a few forms of bonds, above all marriage and family, and leaves little room for others. He saw the task as inventing new forms of relationship, friendship and mutual care. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that the fear of abandonment is especially strong when all your support rests on one or two bonds sanctioned by the norm. But life can be richer: friends, communities, mentors, neighbors. The wider the web of care, the less a single parting threatens everything. This doesn’t cancel the fear, but it gives you more to lean on.
abandonment.practice: Draw a map of your connections: who else, besides those closest to you, is in your life? Mark one connection you would like to strengthen.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is a pain full of silence. Foucault showed that even what is most intimate in us is organized by cultural norms. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that love, too, has its scripts: reciprocity as the norm, “the other half,” the happy ending. Against them, an unreturned feeling looks like a failure. But your feeling is not a failure; it is an experience that doesn’t fit the template. The late Foucault saw life as material to which a person gives form themselves, as an artist does to a work. Unrequited love can become part of that form: it can teach you something about your capacity to feel, about your desires, about what matters to you. It is real, even if there is no answer.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love has taught you — about yourself, not about the other person.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the deepest wounds: you have been stripped of dignity, and it seems as if everyone saw. Foucault wrote a great deal about how power acts through visibility — from the public punishments of the past to modern assessments and rankings put on display. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that humiliation is a technique of power that seeks to make a person “smaller,” to break how they feel about themselves. But it is an act done to you within particular relations of power, not the truth about you. Foucault reminded us: where there is power, there is resistance. Resistance doesn’t have to be loud: it can begin with refusing to accept someone else’s definition of you.
humiliation.practice: Write down how they tried to define you in the moment of humiliation. Then write one word with which you define yourself.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is a very common and heavy feeling. Foucault showed that the body is not only nature but also a place where norms operate. In Discipline and Punish he described “docile bodies” — bodies taught to sit, walk and carry themselves correctly. Later he wrote about “biopower” — power that measures and standardizes life: health, birth rates, life expectancy. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that shame about your body is often not your personal assessment but the imprint of such norms. They have a history: in other eras, bodily ideals were completely different. This knowledge doesn’t dissolve shame at once, but it helps you hear in it someone else’s voice rather than your own truth.
body_shame.practice: Name one bodily “norm” you are ashamed of not meeting. Ask: who invented it, and in what era?

illness.text: Illness is a hard experience: the body lets you down, and your familiar life changes. Your feelings — fear, anger, fatigue — are legitimate. In The Birth of the Clinic, Foucault described the “medical gaze” — the way modern medicine sees a person: as a case, a set of symptoms and readings. This gaze has saved countless lives, but a patient can come to feel that they themselves are disappearing behind the diagnosis. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say: you are more than your diagnosis. The late Foucault studied the ancient “care of the self,” in which care of the body was part of care for one’s whole life — thoughts, relationships, habits. Illness can become an occasion for this kind of gentle care for yourself as a whole.
illness.practice: Describe yourself in three words that have nothing to do with the illness. They are you too.

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a good, legitimate feeling. You accomplished something, and it deserves to be acknowledged. The late Foucault spoke of an “aesthetics of existence” — the idea that life can be built like a work of art, given a form of one’s own. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that healthy pride is the joy of a craftsperson who sees something in their life take shape thanks to their work. What matters is that this is not pride in a place in a ranking or in victory over others, but joy in your own work on yourself and your affairs. Such pride doesn’t need anyone else’s approval. Let yourself be glad — you earned it through your work.
pride.practice: Write down what you did, and answer: what shape has it given to your life?

melancholy.text: Bright sadness is a subtle, sometimes even precious feeling. Foucault paid attention to states that don’t fit the image of a person who is always “productive.” In History of Madness he traced how physicians of different eras explained melancholy in different ways — through “black bile,” through the motion of the “animal spirits,” through the nerves: the concept itself changed its meaning more than once. From Foucault’s point of view, one might say that what today we want to “fix” immediately was understood differently in other times — including as a companion of reflection and fine sensitivity. Your bright sadness doesn’t have to be a problem. You can simply live it as part of your life — quiet and particular.
melancholy.practice: Stay with this mood for a few minutes: by the window, with music, or on a walk. Don’t ask it why it came.
